Use of highly toxic residual pesticides may have to be stopped or considerably modified to protect the bald eagle and other raptors and the brown pelicans which produce thin-shelled or virtually shelless eggs after ingesting amounts of chlorinated hydrocarbon pesticides. The economic impacts will occur from the increased cost of more careful and precise application of the pesticide, substitution of more costly and less effective methods of pest control, or curtailment of the use of such pesticides altogether in certain areas where highly susceptible endangered animals occur. For example, special use regulations may have to be enacted for areas which produce runoff into waterways that harbor fishes on which the endangered eagles feed. Somewhat isolated populations of brown pelicans may be spared undue exposure to pesticides by banning or controlling use of pesticides in the watersheds which supply runoff to the pelican feeding areas. Ultimate restoration of the critically endangered American peregrine falcon will likely require drastic revision of our use of pesticides throughout the nation.
There is a growing body of evidence to suggest that such an alteration in our use of certain pesticides may be required in any advent due to their pervasive effects on the total environment and on man himself. The economic impact of endangered species legislation on this industry then will be minor and secondary to general environemntal considerations.
In summary, short-term economic impacts of the legislation and the program will occur when endangered species are withdrawn from trade or use is curtailed for sport hunting, or fishing and falconry. Long-term impacts will occur when the species is restored to levels consistent with carefully managed cropping. Indirect economic impacts will result from the cost of shifting
